script.opening: "I’ve got this really painful swelling right at the top of my bum crease — it’s red, hot and now it’s started leaking a bit of fluid. I can’t sit down properly, and it’s been building up over a few days. I’ve had a bit of discharge there on and off before. What is it?"

facts.text: Four days, getting bigger. Right at the top of the buttock crease, in the middle — "nowhere near my back passage". Red, hot, very tender, soft in the middle; started leaking yellowish fluid this morning. Can’t sit; lying on his front.
For about a year, "every so often it gets a bit damp and there’s a mark on my boxers". His girlfriend once said there were "little holes" there. Never painful like this.
Felt a bit hot last night; no thermometer. No rigors. Eating and drinking. Redness hasn’t spread beyond the lump. Bowels normal, no bleeding, no pain on opening bowels.
No diabetes known, no immune problems, no medicines, no allergies. BMI about 30. Hairy back. Took ibuprofen this morning.
Sales rep — sits at a desk and drives about 300 miles a week. Lives with his girlfriend, who can drive him. Smokes 10 a day.
Embarrassed and in pain, shifting about. You want antibiotics: "Can I just have antibiotics?" When told it needs draining, be anxious ("A cut? Today?") then agree. Ask how to stop it coming back.

ice.concerns: "It’s embarrassing, and I don’t want it coming back. And I can’t drive for work like this."

cues: "I’ve had a bit of discharge there on and off before" — the underlying sinus.
"Can I just have antibiotics?" — expectation to negotiate: the abscess needs draining.
"I sit and drive a lot" — risk factor and prevention advice.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PILONIDAL DISEASE (midline natal-cleft sinus/pits, hair/friction-related, young hirsute men) and identifies the ACUTE ABSCESS (painful, red, fluctuant, discharging)

Arranges INCISION AND DRAINAGE for the acute abscess (usually via same-day surgical assessment/SDEC; in primary care only if competent and suitable) with analgesia — recognising antibiotics are not a substitute for drainage — after checking observations (NICE NG253 if unwell) and asking about diabetes/immunosuppression
Reserves ANTIBIOTICS for surrounding cellulitis/systemic features rather than treating the abscess with antibiotics alone
REFERS to general/colorectal SURGERY for definitive treatment of the underlying sinus once the acute episode settles (recurrence common)

Advises PREVENTION/hygiene (keep clean/dry, hair removal — limited evidence — and weight discussed without blame) and considers the differential (perianal abscess/fistula, hidradenitis, infected cyst)
Handles a painful, embarrassing problem sensitively, explains the diagnosis and the need for drainage, and checks understanding
Communicates the referral and prevention reasoning clearly and supportively

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent drainage and analgesia, antibiotics only if cellulitis/systemic, surgical referral for definitive care, prevention advice, and return for spreading infection/systemic features — drainage + definitive referral, not antibiotics alone

worked.txt: "This is a pilonidal abscess — an infection in a little pocket at the top of the buttock crease, which forms around trapped hairs. They’re common in younger men, especially with a lot of sitting. The on-off discharge you’ve had before is the underlying sinus, and now it’s flared into an abscess."

"The important thing is that an abscess needs to be drained — letting the pus out is what relieves it. Antibiotics alone won’t fix it. I’ll arrange for you to be seen by the surgical team today to drain it, with good pain relief, and we’ll only add antibiotics if the surrounding skin is spreading-red or you’re feverish."
"Once this settles, I’ll refer you to the surgeons to deal with the underlying sinus properly, because otherwise it tends to recur. There are different procedures and they’ll advise what suits you."

"To reduce recurrence: keep the area clean and dry, and removing the hair around the cleft is widely advised, although the evidence for it is limited. Some people also find it helps to reduce long spells of sitting, and weight can play a part too. These may cut the chance of it coming back."
"I know this is sore and a bit embarrassing — it’s a very common problem and we’ll get you comfortable."
"If the redness spreads, you get a fever or feel unwell, or the pain becomes severe before drainage, contact us urgently. After drainage, we’ll arrange the surgical follow-up."

f.learning: PILONIDAL DISEASE is a sinus/cyst in the midline NATAL CLEFT (top of the buttock crease), typically with one or more midline PITS and related to hair/friction, commonest in young, hirsute men and those who sit a lot or are overweight; intermittent discharge/pits with a now painful, red, fluctuant swelling indicates a PILONIDAL ABSCESS. Distinguish the ACUTE ABSCESS (painful, red, hot, fluctuant, may discharge pus) from a chronic/quiescent sinus — the abscess is the urgent issue. An acute pilonidal abscess needs INCISION AND DRAINAGE, usually through an off-midline incision with definitive surgery deferred (European Society of Coloproctology 2024, international): arrange same-day surgical assessment (drainage in primary care only if competent, equipped and the abscess is suitable) with analgesia (paracetamol and, if suitable, ibuprofen at BNF doses), after checking observations face to face (NICE NG253 if systemically unwell) and asking about diabetes or immunosuppression, recognising that ANTIBIOTICS are NOT a substitute for drainage and should be reserved for surrounding cellulitis or systemic features (NICE NG141) — an undrained abscess will not settle on antibiotics alone. For the underlying SINUS (the recurrent problem), refer to general/colorectal surgery for definitive management once the acute episode settles (the surgeon chooses minimally invasive or excisional options; recurrence after drainage alone is common, so definitive care matters; asymptomatic pits need no operation). Advise prevention and hygiene — keep the area clean and dry, and hair removal around the cleft is widely advised though the evidence is limited, with weight discussed sensitively — and consider the differential (perianal abscess/fistula closer to the anus, hidradenitis suppurativa with other flexures, infected sebaceous cyst). Handle a painful, embarrassing problem sensitively, arrange drainage rather than antibiotics alone, refer for definitive treatment, and safety-net for spreading infection/systemic features.

knowledge.guideline: [1] European Society of Coloproctology guidelines for the management of pilonidal disease, BJS 2024;111(10):znae237 (international) · [2] NICE NG141 Cellulitis and erysipelas: antimicrobial prescribing (2019) · [3] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over (2025)
knowledge.summary: A tender, fluctuant, discharging swelling in the midline natal cleft of a young hairy man with a history of on-off discharge is an acute pilonidal abscess on a chronic sinus. The abscess needs incision and drainage, not antibiotics alone; definitive treatment of the sinus is planned once the inflammation has settled.

points.t: Pilonidal disease is a chronic sinus in the natal cleft, usually with one or more midline pits containing hair. It is commonest in young men, with hirsutism, prolonged sitting and a raised BMI as associations. It may be asymptomatic, cause recurrent discharge, or present as an acute abscess.

A painful, red, swollen, fluctuant lump in the cleft, sometimes discharging pus. ESCP [1]: manage the acute abscess by incision and drainage, usually through an incision placed off the midline, and defer definitive surgery until the inflammation has settled. In most areas this is done through same-day surgical assessment.

Antibiotics do not replace drainage. Consider them only for spreading cellulitis around the abscess or systemic features, choosing the agent and dose from NICE NG141 [2] and the BNF, and reassess if not improving.

Check temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and mental state. Use NICE NG253 [3] to decide the urgency of assessment if he is systemically unwell. Ask about diabetes or immunosuppression, which raise the threshold for urgent referral.

Perianal abscess or fistula-in-ano (nearer the anal verge, with pain on defecation), hidradenitis suppurativa (recurrent nodules and tracts in the axillae, groins or perineum), an infected epidermoid cyst, and a boil. Midline pits are the discriminating sign for pilonidal disease.

Refer routinely to general or colorectal surgery for the chronic sinus once the abscess has settled; recurrence after drainage alone is common and the surgeon chooses between minimally invasive and excisional options [1]. Asymptomatic pits need no operation. Keeping the cleft clean and dry and removing hair from the area are widely advised; the evidence for hair removal is limited.
Paracetamol and, if suitable, ibuprofen at BNF doses while awaiting drainage. Check for contraindications to NSAIDs.

model.text: Hello Mr Reilly, I’m Dr Shah. Come in, and sit or stand, whichever is more comfortable. What’s been happening?
model.why: Open start, notices he cannot sit

model.text: I’ve got this really painful swelling right at the top of my bum crease. It’s red, hot and now it’s started leaking a bit of fluid. I can’t sit down properly, and it’s been building up over a few days. I’ve had a bit of discharge there on and off before. What is it?
That sounds very sore. I’ll ask a few questions, have a look if that’s okay, and then we’ll work out what it is and how to get you comfortable.
When you say you’ve had discharge there before, what was that like?
model.why: Follows the cue of previous discharge

model.text: Every so often it gets a bit damp and there’s a mark on my boxers. It never hurt like this though.
Is the swelling right in the middle of the crease, or closer to your back passage?
Right at the top, where the crease starts. Nowhere near my backside.
Any pain when you open your bowels, or any bleeding or change in your bowels?
model.why: Screens for perianal abscess or fistula

model.text: No, that’s all normal.
Have you had fevers, shivers, or felt generally unwell?
Not that I’ve noticed. It’s just really sore.
Do you get painful lumps anywhere else, like your armpits or groin?
No, just this.
Do you have diabetes or any condition or medicine that lowers your immunity? And any allergies to medicines?
model.why: Risk factors for severe infection; allergy before any prescription

model.text: No, nothing like that. No allergies I know of.
How is this affecting work and day-to-day life?
I sit at a desk and drive a lot for work. I just can’t do either at the moment.
What have you been thinking it might be? And is anything worrying you about it?
Some kind of abscess, I guess. Honestly it’s a bit embarrassing. I just want it sorted, and I don’t want it coming back.

Thank you for telling me. It’s a very common problem and nothing to be embarrassed about. I need to look at the area. Would you like a chaperone? (Examines with consent: temperature, pulse and blood pressure normal. Tender, red, fluctuant swelling just off the midline at the top of the natal cleft, a little discharge, and small midline pits. The redness is limited to the swelling, and the perianal area looks normal.)
model.why: Chaperone, observations and focused examination including the perianal area

model.text: This is a pilonidal abscess. There’s a small channel under the skin in the crease, called a pilonidal sinus, which forms around trapped hairs. That explains the on-off discharge. Now it has become infected and filled with pus.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and links it to his history

model.text: Can I just have antibiotics?

Antibiotics on their own won’t clear a collection of pus like this. It needs a small cut to let the pus out, and that is what gets rid of the pain. The redness isn’t spreading and you’re not feverish, so antibiotics aren’t needed at the moment.
model.why: Drainage, not antibiotics alone; antibiotics only for cellulitis or systemic features

model.text: A cut? Today?
Yes. I’ll speak to the surgical team today so it can be drained, usually under local anaesthetic. They’ll explain how to look after the wound.

Until then, regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, if it suits you, will take the edge off. Once it has healed, I’ll refer you to the surgeons in clinic to treat the channel itself, because otherwise these often come back. There are several options and they’ll go through them with you.
model.why: Analgesia and routine referral for definitive care

model.text: Is there anything I can do so it doesn’t happen again?

Keeping the area clean and dry helps, and many people remove the hair around the crease, although the evidence for that is limited. Breaking up long spells of sitting may help too. For work, you can self-certify for the first week and I can give you a fit note after that if you need it. Please don’t drive if the pain stops you from driving safely.
model.why: Prevention advice without blame; work and driving

model.text: That’s useful, thanks.
If the redness spreads, you get a fever or shivers, or you feel unwell before you’re seen, ring 111 or go to A&E. So, what’s the plan in your own words?
Get it drained today, painkillers, then the surgeons for the channel. Come back if it spreads or I get a fever.
Exactly right. I’ll see you after the drainage to check the wound and make the clinic referral.

social.t: Sitting and driving are both painful. He can self-certify for up to 7 days; a fit note can cover the period after drainage or surgery.
Many people delay seeking help for problems near the buttocks. Normalise it and offer a chaperone.

legal.t: No DVLA notification is needed. Advise him not to drive while pain or strong analgesia affects his ability to control the vehicle, including an emergency stop.
GMC guidance on intimate examinations: explain, gain consent, offer a chaperone and record who was present.

professional.t: Prescribing antibiotics instead of drainage is poor care and adds to resistance. Record why antibiotics were or were not given (NICE NG141).
Drain in primary care only if competent, equipped and the abscess is suitable; otherwise refer to same-day surgical assessment.

community.t: After drainage the wound is usually packed or dressed; practice or community nurses often continue the dressings.
Local same-day emergency care (SDEC) or on-call surgical team for drainage; routine general or colorectal surgical clinic for the sinus.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, tachycardia or feeling very unwell (NICE NG253)
Swelling near the anal verge or pain on defecation, suggesting a perianal abscess or fistula
psychosocial: Desk work and driving for work
ice: Concern: embarrassment and it coming back

playbook.diagnosis: “This is a pilonidal abscess: an infected pocket at the top of the buttock crease, sitting on a small channel that has been there a while.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Hairs get trapped in the skin of the crease and form a little tunnel. That explains the on-off leaking. Now it has become infected and filled with pus, which is why it hurts so much.”

management.reflectIce: “You said it’s embarrassing and you don’t want it back. It’s very common, and the plan deals with both today’s abscess and the channel underneath.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a chaperone, avoid blaming language about weight or hair, and cover work and driving.
sharedPlan: Same-day incision and drainage via the surgical team (or in primary care only if competent and suitable)
Paracetamol and ibuprofen at BNF doses; antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis or systemic features (NICE NG141)
Routine general or colorectal surgical referral for the sinus once settled; hygiene and hair advice
safetyNet: Spreading redness, fever, rigors or feeling unwell: 111 or A&E the same day
Review after drainage to check the wound and make the surgical referral
Return if discharge or swelling recurs

pitfalls.intro: This station is about one clear decision: an abscess needs draining. Candidates lose marks by prescribing antibiotics alone, by not examining, and by forgetting the sinus that caused it.

items.fail: Treating the abscess with antibiotics alone.
items.why: A collection of pus needs incision and drainage (ESCP 2024, international); antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis or systemic features.
items.fix: Arrange same-day drainage and explain why.

items.fail: Not examining, or not checking observations.
items.why: Fluctuance, cellulitis, the pits and systemic signs decide the plan and the urgency.
items.fix: Offer a chaperone, check observations and inspect the cleft and perianal area.

items.why: The history of on-off discharge shows a chronic sinus; drainage alone often leads to recurrence.
items.fix: Refer for definitive treatment once the abscess settles.

items.why: A perianal abscess or fistula lies near the anal verge and has a different surgical pathway.
items.fix: Ask about site and bowel symptoms and examine the perianal area.

items.fail: Blaming his weight or body hair.
items.why: He already feels embarrassed; blame closes the conversation.
items.fix: Normalise it and give prevention advice neutrally.

items.fail: Vague safety-net with no plan for work.
items.why: He cannot sit or drive, and infection can spread.
items.fix: Name spreading redness and fever, cover self-certification and driving, and book review.

timeMap.d: Let him describe the swelling and the past discharge. Notice he cannot sit.
Site relative to the anus, bowel symptoms, fever, lumps elsewhere, diabetes or immunosuppression, allergy.
Work and driving; name the embarrassment and the fear of recurrence.
Chaperone, observations, pits, fluctuance, cellulitis, perianal area.
Pilonidal abscess; drainage today, not antibiotics alone; analgesia; later surgical referral; prevention; fit note; safety-net and teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Gives a course of antibiotics and sends him home; does not examine or check observations; misses the underlying sinus; no plan for definitive care.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a pilonidal abscess, examines with a chaperone, arranges drainage, gives analgesia, refers for the sinus later and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses the history of on-off discharge to explain the sinus; distinguishes it from a perianal abscess by site and bowel symptoms; explains clearly why antibiotics are not the treatment; handles embarrassment warmly; covers work and driving; checks the plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Take these antibiotics and it should settle.”
avoid.instead: “Pus needs to be let out. Antibiotics alone won’t clear it, so I’m arranging for it to be drained today.”
avoid.why: An undrained abscess does not resolve on antibiotics and delays relief.

avoid.instead: “It forms around trapped hairs in the crease. Keeping the area clean, dry and free of hair may help stop it coming back.”
avoid.why: Blaming language damages rapport; the same advice can be given neutrally.

avoid.instead: “Drainage treats the abscess. The channel underneath often causes more trouble, so I’ll refer you to have that treated.”
avoid.why: Recurrence after drainage alone is common, so definitive care needs planning.

Routine surgical referral for the sinus once settled; hygiene and hair advice; work and driving addressed.
Clear safety-net for spreading redness or fever; teach-back; review after drainage.

social.t: Sitting and driving are both painful. He can self-certify for up to 7 days; a fit note can cover the period after drainage or surgery.
Many people delay seeking help for problems near the buttocks. Normalise it and offer a chaperone.

legal.t: No DVLA notification is needed. Advise him not to drive while pain or strong analgesia affects his ability to control the vehicle, including an emergency stop.
GMC guidance on intimate examinations: explain, gain consent, offer a chaperone and record who was present.

professional.t: Prescribing antibiotics instead of drainage is poor care and adds to resistance. Record why antibiotics were or were not given (NICE NG141).
Drain in primary care only if competent, equipped and the abscess is suitable; otherwise refer to same-day surgical assessment.

community.t: After drainage the wound is usually packed or dressed; practice or community nurses often continue the dressings.
Local same-day emergency care (SDEC) or on-call surgical team for drainage; routine general or colorectal surgical clinic for the sinus.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, tachycardia or feeling very unwell (NICE NG253)
Swelling near the anal verge or pain on defecation, suggesting a perianal abscess or fistula
psychosocial: Desk work and driving for work
ice: Concern: embarrassment and it coming back

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is a pilonidal abscess: an infected pocket at the top of the buttock crease, sitting on a small channel that has been there a while.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Hairs get trapped in the skin of the crease and form a little tunnel. That explains the on-off leaking. Now it has become infected and filled with pus, which is why it hurts so much.”

management.reflectIce: “You said it’s embarrassing and you don’t want it back. It’s very common, and the plan deals with both today’s abscess and the channel underneath.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a chaperone, avoid blaming language about weight or hair, and cover work and driving.
sharedPlan: Same-day incision and drainage via the surgical team (or in primary care only if competent and suitable)
Paracetamol and ibuprofen at BNF doses; antibiotics only for spreading cellulitis or systemic features (NICE NG141)
Routine general or colorectal surgical referral for the sinus once settled; hygiene and hair advice
safetyNet: Spreading redness, fever, rigors or feeling unwell: 111 or A&E the same day
Review after drainage to check the wound and make the surgical referral
Return if discharge or swelling recurs

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about one clear decision: an abscess needs draining. Candidates lose marks by prescribing antibiotics alone, by not examining, and by forgetting the sinus that caused it.

items.fail: Treating the abscess with antibiotics alone.
items.why: A collection of pus needs incision and drainage (ESCP 2024, international); antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis or systemic features.
items.fix: Arrange same-day drainage and explain why.

items.fail: Not examining, or not checking observations.
items.why: Fluctuance, cellulitis, the pits and systemic signs decide the plan and the urgency.
items.fix: Offer a chaperone, check observations and inspect the cleft and perianal area.

items.why: The history of on-off discharge shows a chronic sinus; drainage alone often leads to recurrence.
items.fix: Refer for definitive treatment once the abscess settles.

items.why: A perianal abscess or fistula lies near the anal verge and has a different surgical pathway.
items.fix: Ask about site and bowel symptoms and examine the perianal area.

items.fail: Blaming his weight or body hair.
items.why: He already feels embarrassed; blame closes the conversation.
items.fix: Normalise it and give prevention advice neutrally.

items.fail: Vague safety-net with no plan for work.
items.why: He cannot sit or drive, and infection can spread.
items.fix: Name spreading redness and fever, cover self-certification and driving, and book review.
